newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire prompts S.Africa Rwanda arms sale review.
newsitem.headline: Zaire prompts S.Africa Rwanda arms sale review.

text.p: South Africa said on Friday it would review a decision made in September to lift an arms ban on Rwanda, the Central African country whose troops have intervened this week in the ethnic fighting in neighbouring Zaire.
Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad said the arms sales, worth an estimated 86.8 million rand ($18.5 million), were under review.
"As the conflict has now escalated with allegations of Rwandan troops being involved outside the borders, we have to review it in that context," he told a parliamentary committee.

"The dilemma we were facing is that those who were responsible for the genocide of over a million people are still the people who are being trained and receiving arms and are launching incursions into Rwanda."
Foreign armies have denied fighting alongside Tutsi rebels in Zaire but Rwanda has said it sent troops on an incursion this week after artillery and machinegun exchanges across its border.
The fighting in Zaire between the rebels and the Zairean army spilled over into Rwanda on Friday, with mortar bombs landing in the border town of Gisenyi.
South African officials have refused to detail the type of arms sold to Rwanda, describing them merely as "defensive".
"We have a strong commitment from the government of Rwanda that South African arms will not be used in any action across the borders of Rwanda," Pahad said.
"If it comes to light that Rwandan forces are using South African arms outside their borders then will have to review that situation."

President Nelson Mandela on Friday defended the arms sales to Rwanda and told reporters in Pretoria that he "totally rejected" criticism of the decision in September to lift its ban on arms sales to Rwanda.

"I will not allow that army to come back and massacre people," Mandela said, referring to Hutu factions, including the remains of the army of the deposed government, responsible for massacres of Tutsis in Rwanda.
Mandela said the United Nations had asked South Africa to get involved in efforts to defuse the war in eastern Zaire.
"Anything within our capacity and legal system we will do," he said, adding that he would await the outcome of a regional summit of seven African states in Kenya on Tuesday.

"I am not keen to act independently of structures that have been set up," he said. "In Africa we have a very competent core of leaders. It would be a mistake to expect South Africa to act unilaterally," Mandela said.
Asked about South African contributing troops to a peacekeeping force, Pahad said:
"The specific manifestation of how this comes into being is the question... we are not cold on the idea but are seeking more clarification.
"It is a major initiative which has to be discussed, and we are not opposed to it in principle."
